Key Takeaways

David Tepper's Appaloosa filed its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30 on Nov. 16. It showed $7.56 billion of US stocks in 24 positions.

Among its positions of 2% or more, Wall Street sees the most upside in Micron, Alibaba, Oracle, SpaceX and Lam Research, with average targets 72% to 119% above today's prices.

Four of the five have fallen 16% to 36% since Sept. 30, so much of that upside comes from the selloff.

Micron, Appaloosa's biggest position, is the one the numbers back best, though memory stocks have looked this cheap at past peaks.

David Tepper doesn't spread his money thin. His Appaloosa, which manages $20.40 billion in all, held just 24 US stocks worth $7.56 billion at Sept. 30, according to its 13F for the quarter, filed Nov. 16.

Most of his big bets have taken a beating since. Here are the five of his positions of 2% or more where Wall Street sees the most upside: Micron (MU:NASDAQ), Alibaba (BABA:NYSE), Oracle (ORCL:NYSE), SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) and Lam Research (LRCX:NASDAQ).

1. Micron: Tepper's biggest bet got bigger

Micron is Appaloosa's largest holding by far: 1.25 million shares worth $1.33 billion at Sept. 30, or 17.6% of its 13F stocks, after it added 28% more shares in the quarter. The stock is down 33% since then, even though Micron's revenue more than tripled to $133.2 billion in fiscal 2026 and it out-earned Apple last quarter.

Analysts have raised their numbers all year. Over the past 12 months, the average target has climbed from about $213 to $1,562, which is 119% above today's price:

Micron Technology (MU): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

By our math, $1,562 is under 8x analysts' fiscal 2028 earnings estimate. Micron has usually traded at about 10x since 2014. Today it trades at about 4x forward earnings. Its December report covers the quarter that management calls this fiscal year's low point for gross margin.

TIKR tracks 50 analysts on Micron. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Micron, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Micron's Analyst Ratings

2. Alibaba: the cloud is booming, but the cash isn't there yet

Appaloosa trimmed its Alibaba stake by 7% in the third quarter, to 1.85 million shares worth $199 million, or 2.6% of its 13F stocks. The stock is down 19% since Sept. 30 and 52% below its 52-week high.

The cloud business is doing its part. Its revenue grew 45% in the June quarter to RMB 48.4 billion, and its adjusted EBITA margin rose to 11.6% from 7.2% a year earlier. But the AI apps unit lost RMB 13.9 billion in the same quarter, and free cash flow was an outflow of RMB 44.7 billion. Meanwhile, the US keeps tightening its chip curbs on Chinese AI companies.

Anthropic's planned US$1.4t IPO has put fast growing, high conviction businesses back in the spotlight. Investors are watching how much value can build when revenue expansion and insider belief line up. That combination can be hard to find, which creates real FOMO when it shows up. This article breaks down three fast growing, insider backed US stocks from our screener that fit that profile today.

The three stocks highlighted here offer a compelling starting point if you want exposure to fast growing businesses where both analysts and insiders see meaningful potential ahead. However, if you want the pick of this theme, these 52 high growth high conviction stocks are the best of the best.

Arista Networks (ANET)

Overview: Arista Networks builds EOS powered networking hardware and software that connect AI, cloud, and data center environments for large enterprise customers.

Operations: Arista generates about US$11.9b of revenue from its Computer Networks segment, with most sales coming from customers in the United States.

Market Cap: US$236.3b

Arista Networks fits the Fast Growing Stocks With High Insider Ownership theme because its EOS based data center and AI networking products are central to how big cloud and hyperscale customers handle rapidly rising AI traffic. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St captures how that focus shapes expectations.

"Accelerated adoption of AI and machine learning workloads continues to increase demand for high-bandwidth, low-latency networking infrastructure, and Arista Networks is now guiding AI fabrics revenue of at least US$3.5b to US$3.6b in 2026 with Etherlink already used by more than 100 customers, which could support multi-year revenue growth and earnings expansion."

What happens if a single assumption about future AI buildout intensity shifts and changes how that expansion flows through to profitability?

If that profitability swing is what you are weighing, the full narrative for Arista Networks shows how AI fabrics, capital intensity, and insider conviction could be accelerating in different directions.

Overview: Oracle provides cloud software, databases, and infrastructure that help enterprises run core finance, HR, operations, and industry specific applications worldwide.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Nvidia reported results on Tuesday after the close. Sales were $115.8 billion in the quarter to October, double a year ago. Nvidia's outlook for the January quarter is $130 billion. The stock closed Tuesday at $155.46, down 0.4%, before the report.

Most coverage will focus on those two numbers. This article looks at a different one: what customers owe.

On Tuesday morning, Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash named three lines to read in this report. They were operating cash, receivables and investment gains. Here is how each one came in.

Did The Cash Catch Up?

Mostly, yes. In the quarter to October, Nvidia booked $65.3 billion of profit. It took in $48.3 billion of cash from its operations. That is 74% of its profit. In July, it was 40%.

Free cash flow is the cash left after capital spending. It was $43.8 billion, more than double July's $21.4 billion.

The table shows the swing. Cash as a share of profit is back to 74%, the same as a year earlier.

That removes one of the worst cases in Tuesday's article. That case used Nvidia's free cash flow at July's pace. It applied the price investors paid for each dollar of free cash at the December 2018 low. The result was about $83 a share. At October's pace, the same price gives about $170. That is above Tuesday's close.

One quarter of cash moved that value for Nvidia from about $83 a share to about $170. If Nvidia is a big part of your wealth, so are its risk and its tax bill. Our partner advisory firm offers a free 30-minute strategy review covering a floor under losses and a lower-tax way out. Map your exit options.

So Why Do Customers Owe $81 Billion?

This is the line that got worse. Receivables are money customers owe for chips already delivered. At Nvidia, they rose to $81.0 billion at the end of the October quarter, from $63.1 billion in July. That is $18.0 billion more in one quarter.

To compare across years, we turn receivables into days of sales: receivables divided by the quarter's sales, times 91 days. By that measure, customers owed about 64 days of sales. That is up from 60 in July and 45 in April.

Nvidia's own record goes back to 2001. In that time, customers owed it more than 64 days of sales in only three quarters. The closest case below those is October 2018, at 63 days.

Key Takeaways

Oracle's credit default swaps hit record wides on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia reported $115.8 billion of quarterly revenue.

Guy Adami called Oracle the weak link among the hyperscalers, and its numbers back him up.

Analysts expect Oracle's free cash flow, negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, to stay negative through fiscal 2028.

Oracle's December report, with net cash capex against its $70 billion cap, is the next test.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) should have been one of the big winners from Nvidia's quarter.

Nvidia reported $115.8 billion of third-quarter revenue on Tuesday night, up 103% from a year earlier. Interim CEO Colette Kress said that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong."

Oracle rents out exactly that kind of computing capacity. But the credit market didn't budge: Oracle's credit default swaps were back at record wides the same day.

On the RiskReversal Pod after Tuesday's close, Guy Adami, co-founder of RiskReversal Media and one of CNBC's "Fast Money" traders, singled out one AI stock:

"Oracle is the weak link on the hyperscaler space, and if all this stuff doesn't work, Oracle's dead."

Harsh. But with the stock about 65% below its September 2025 high, the market seems to agree with him.

Oracle has to pay for the build first

Oracle has to build and equip its data centers before its contracts turn into cash. Its free cash flow went from $11.8 billion in fiscal 2024 to negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026 (Oracle's fiscal years end in May). Analysts expect it to get worse before it gets better:

Oracle (ORCL): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to May) (TIKR)

Even the fiscal 2029 estimate is well below the "$30 billion plus" that CFO Hilary Maxson has promised for that year.

In fiscal 2026, Oracle's capital expenditures were $23.7 billion more than the cash its operations brought in:

Oracle (ORCL): cash from operations vs. capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2022-2026 (years to May) (TIKR)

And Oracle expects to spend $90 billion to $95 billion this fiscal year.

TIKR tracks 42 analysts on Oracle. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

So Oracle borrows

Oracle's total debt, leases included, more than doubled from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026:

Oracle (ORCL): total debt, $ billions, fiscal 2022-2026 (years to May) (TIKR)

It reached $169.1 billion by Aug. 31, and that was before this month's raise. On Nov. 2, Oracle sold $10 billion of stock at $116 a share and $10 billion of notes, with an average coupon of about 7.8%.

Bond investors noticed. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps were at 292 basis points on Nov. 2, up 265% in a year. S&P already cut Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, in July.

Picture a new AI data center, as an example. The chips are in, but the utility says the grid connection will take years. So the owner sets up a small power plant outside. It is a row of fuel-cell boxes that turn natural gas into electricity. Boxes like these are Bloom Energy's business.

On Tuesday evening, Nvidia guided to $130 billion of sales for its January quarter. All of those chips will need power.

Yet investors now pay far less for Bloom. One yardstick is price-to-sales, the market value divided by the last four quarters of sales. Bloom trades at 13.4 times sales, down 67% from 40.1 times on June 22.

Analysts still expect fast growth. The average estimate of 20 analysts puts 2027 sales at $7.27 billion. That is 63% above the $4.47 billion they expect for 2026.

Was 40 Times Sales Ever Real?

No, it was a spike. Bloom began this year at 11.3 times sales. Then its stock nearly quadrupled in under six months, from $86.89 to $345.85 on June 22. By July 29 it had lost 53%. At Tuesday's close of $173.46, it is still up nearly 100% for the year.

A 53% fall between June 22 and July 29 is hard to sit through. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. For every dollar its benchmark lost, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio lost about 81 cents on average. It holds 30 quality stocks in equal weight. See the HQ record.

Most of the AI-power group made the same round trip this year. Vertiv went from 6.4 times sales to 13.3, then back to 5.6. Bloom's 13.4 is still the highest in the group. It is more than twice Vertiv's.

Why Did The Stock Fall After Its Best Quarter?

In the quarter to September, Bloom's sales rose 138% from a year earlier, to $1.24 billion. It reported $250 million of profit. Yet the stock fell 19% from Oct 21 to Oct 23. That includes an 11% drop on the day after its report on the evening of Oct 22.

Over five quarters, Bloom's operating margin, the share of sales kept as operating profit, rose from 1.5% to 18.2%. But operating cash, the cash the business brings in, went from $418 million in December to minus $27 million in September.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Salesforce stock fell 9.5% on Tuesday, Nov 17, to close at $194.52. It was the stock's largest one-day fall since May 30, 2024, when it dropped 19.7%. The S&P 500 lost 1.0% the same day. ServiceNow fell 6.5% and Adobe fell 4.2%.

Why did it fall? MarketWatch reported that a series of technology outages left investors worried that software companies could be "particularly vulnerable" to AI misuse, citing an analyst. Invezz tied the fall to the same outages and to worries about software reliability and security. The Motley Fool said security jitters and fears that AI could replace software hit the whole group. Business Insider reported the same day that Salesforce has started cutting more jobs. No outlet showed that the job cuts moved the stock.

Most coverage focuses on the fear that AI could replace software. This article looks at cash. At Tuesday's close, Salesforce traded at 10.5 times the free cash it produced over the past year. Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment. Measured the same way at each quarter end since 2010, only two readings were lower. So the stock is near its cheapest on cash in that record, but this is not a record low.

How Cheap Is Salesforce On Cash?

The price of 10.5 times cash flow equals a free cash flow yield of 9.5%. Across 67 quarter ends since 2010, the middle reading was 40.2 times. The lowest was just under 10 times, at the end of July 2026.

The stock got cheap quickly. It traded at 19.2 times cash flow at the end of October 2025. That fell to 13.8 times by the end of January 2026 and to 10.5 times by the end of April, a touch below Tuesday's reading. The shares are down 26.6% this year. They closed 27.4% below their 52-week high and 47.1% below their record close of $367.87 on Dec 4, 2024. Tuesday's close was the lowest since Aug 17.

One peer is cheaper than Salesforce on this measure and one is more expensive. Here is the same measure for the two software stocks that fell with it.

The Business Behind The Price
